note.explanation: The cell cycle is the sequence of events in which a cell grows, copies its DNA and divides. Mitosis makes two genetically identical cells with the same chromosome number; meiosis makes cells with half the chromosome number and creates genetic variation.
examples: In the S phase, DNA is copied so each chromosome has two sister chromatids.
In mitosis, sister chromatids separate during anaphase. In meiosis, homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis-I and sister chromatids separate in meiosis-II.
note.checkAnswer: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase of mitosis; in meiosis they separate during anaphase-II.
note.simple: A cell first grows and copies its DNA. Then it divides. Mitosis makes two matching cells; meiosis makes cells with half the chromosomes.
note.checkQuestion: When do sister chromatids separate in mitosis?
note.title: The cell cycle and cell division
steps: Interphase: the cell grows during G1, copies DNA during S, and prepares for division during G2.
Mitosis: the nucleus divides through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm divides to form two daughter cells.
Meiosis: two nuclear divisions produce cells with half the original chromosome number; crossing over helps create variation.
note.answer: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. Meiosis produces cells with half the chromosome number and contributes to genetic variation.

mcqs.stem: Q4.1. In which phase of cell cycle, maximum growth occurs in cell?
rationales: M phase is when the cell divides, not when maximum growth occurs.
S phase is when DNA is replicated.
G1 phase is the main growth phase of interphase.
G2 phase is mainly preparation for cell division.

mcqs.stem: Q4.2. In which phase of cell cycle, the chromosomes duplicate?
rationales: Mitosis separates duplicated chromosomes into daughter nuclei.
G1 is mainly a growth phase before DNA replication.
G2 follows DNA replication and prepares the cell for division.
S phase is when DNA is replicated and chromosomes duplicate.

options: It results in genetically identical daughter cells.
The chromosome number is halved in daughter cells.
It results in the formation of two daughter cells.
mcqs.stem: Q4.3. Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of mitosis?
rationales: Mitosis commonly occurs in somatic cells.
Mitosis normally produces genetically identical daughter cells.
Halving the chromosome number is characteristic of meiosis, not mitosis.
Mitosis followed by cytokinesis produces two daughter cells.

mcqs.stem: Q4.4. At which stage of mitosis chromosomes line up in the centre?
rationales: In prophase, chromosomes condense and the spindle forms.
In metaphase, chromosomes line up at the cell's centre.
In anaphase, sister chromatids move towards opposite poles.
In telophase, new nuclear membranes form around the chromosome sets.

mcqs.stem: Q4.5. If you observe a cell in which nuclear membrane is reforming around two sets of chromosomes, what stage of cell cycle is this?
rationales: In anaphase, chromatids are moving to opposite poles.
In telophase, nuclear membranes reform around the two chromosome sets.
In prophase, the nuclear membrane breaks down rather than reforms.
In metaphase, chromosomes line up at the cell's centre.

mcqs.stem: Q4.6. How does the centrosome contribute to mitosis?
rationales: DNA replication occurs during S phase, not as a centrosome function in mitosis.
The centrosome organizes the microtubules that form the mitotic spindle.
The nuclear envelope reforms around chromosomes during telophase.
The centrosome's key role in mitosis is spindle organization, not organelle duplication.

mcqs.stem: Q4.7. Centrosomes make mitotic spindle in:
rationales: Animal cells use centrosomes to organize the mitotic spindle.
Most plant cells lack centrosomes, though they form a spindle by other means.
Prokaryotic cells do not undergo mitosis.
Because prokaryotes and most plant cells do not use centrosomes to make the spindle, this is not true of all cells.

mcqs.stem: Q4.8. An organism has 4 pairs of chromosomes. After meiosis-I, how many chromosomes and chromatids will be present in each daughter cell?
rationales: This gives the original chromosome number and too many chromatids for each meiosis-I daughter cell.
Four chromosomes remain in each daughter cell, each still made of two chromatids, giving eight chromatids.
The chromosomes have not yet lost their sister chromatids after meiosis-I.
This incorrectly keeps the original diploid chromosome number in each daughter cell.

mcqs.stem: Q4.9. Which event is unique to meiosis but not mitosis?
rationales: DNA replication occurs before both mitosis and meiosis.
Chromosomes align during both kinds of division.
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.
Nuclear division occurs in both mitosis and meiosis.

mcqs.stem: Q4.10. Why is meiosis-II necessary after meiosis-I?
rationales: Chromosome replication takes place before meiosis-I, not between the two meiotic divisions.
The reduction in chromosome number occurs in meiosis-I.
Meiosis-II separates the sister chromatids of each chromosome.
Genetic recombination is associated with crossing over in meiosis-I, not the main purpose of meiosis-II.

written.text: Q4.1. Enlist the events that occur during the G1 phase of interphase?
written.finalAnswer: The cell grows, synthesizes proteins and RNA, and duplicates or increases its organelles.

rubric.why: Growth is the main event of G1.
rubric.how: Mention growth of the cell.

rubric.why: G1 includes synthesis and increase of cell components.
rubric.how: Mention protein/RNA synthesis or organelle increase.

modelAnswer: The cell increases in size and carries out normal metabolic activities.
It synthesizes proteins and RNA and increases or duplicates organelles.

written.text: Q4.2. What is the main purpose of the S phase in the cell cycle?
written.finalAnswer: DNA is replicated, so each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids.

rubric.why: The defining event of S phase is DNA replication.
rubric.how: State that DNA is copied or replicated.

rubric.why: Replication leaves each chromosome with two sister chromatids.
rubric.how: Explain that each chromosome now has two sister chromatids.

modelAnswer: DNA is replicated during the S phase.
As a result, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids.

written.text: Q4.3. During which phase of mitosis sister chromatids separate?

rubric.why: Anaphase is the stage when sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles.
rubric.how: Write anaphase.

modelAnswer: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase.

written.text: Q4.4. How does crossing over contribute to genetic variation in meiosis?
written.finalAnswer: Crossing over exchanges segments of DNA between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, producing new combinations of alleles.

rubric.why: The exchange occurs between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes.
rubric.how: Name homologous chromosomes or their non-sister chromatids.

rubric.why: The exchange creates new genetic combinations.
rubric.description: Explain the effect of crossing over.
rubric.how: State that it increases genetic variation or creates new combinations.

modelAnswer: During prophase-I, non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes exchange corresponding segments of DNA.
This produces new combinations of alleles and increases genetic variation.

written.text: Q4.6. How is cytokinesis in animal cell different from plant cell?
written.finalAnswer: In animal cells, a cleavage furrow pinches the cell into two. In plant cells, a cell plate forms between the daughter nuclei and develops into a new cell wall.

rubric.why: Animal cells divide by the inward pinching of the cell membrane.
rubric.how: Mention a cleavage furrow or pinching.

rubric.why: The plant cell plate develops into a cell wall between daughter cells.
rubric.how: Mention cell-plate formation.

modelAnswer: In an animal cell, the cell membrane forms a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell into two.
In a plant cell, a cell plate forms between the daughter nuclei and develops into a new cell wall.

written.text: Q4.7. What is the difference between prophase of mitosis and prophase-I of meiosis-I?
written.finalAnswer: In mitotic prophase, chromosomes condense but homologous chromosomes do not pair and crossing over does not occur. In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids.

rubric.why: Pairing of homologous chromosomes distinguishes prophase-I.
rubric.how: Mention pairing or synapsis of homologous chromosomes.

rubric.why: Crossing over occurs in prophase-I but not ordinary mitotic prophase.
rubric.description: State the key difference in crossing over.
rubric.how: Mention that crossing over occurs in prophase-I, not mitosis.

modelAnswer: In prophase of mitosis, chromosomes condense, but homologous chromosomes do not pair and crossing over does not occur.
In prophase-I of meiosis-I, homologous chromosomes pair, and crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids.

written.text: Q4.8. How does meiosis differ from mitosis in terms of chromosome number?
written.finalAnswer: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number in daughter cells, whereas meiosis halves it.

rubric.why: Mitosis produces daughter cells with the parent's chromosome number.
rubric.how: Say that mitosis maintains the chromosome number.

rubric.why: Meiosis reduces chromosome number by half.
rubric.how: Say that meiosis halves the chromosome number.

modelAnswer: Mitosis maintains the chromosome number in the daughter cells.
Meiosis reduces the chromosome number by half.

written.text: Q4.1. Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis.
written.finalAnswer: Prophase: chromosomes condense and the spindle forms. Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclear membranes reform around the two chromosome sets.

rubric.why: Prophase begins the sequence of mitotic nuclear division.
rubric.how: State that chromosomes condense and the spindle forms.

rubric.why: The chromosome arrangement at the cell centre is a key identifying event.
rubric.how: State that chromosomes line up at the equator.

rubric.why: Chromatid separation is the defining event of anaphase.
rubric.how: State that sister chromatids move to opposite poles.

rubric.why: Telophase completes nuclear division by rebuilding nuclei.
rubric.how: State that nuclear membranes reform around the chromosome sets.

modelAnswer: Prophase: Chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes. The spindle forms and the nuclear membrane breaks down.
Metaphase: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes, which line up at the equator of the cell.
Anaphase: Sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.
Telophase: Chromosomes reach the poles, and nuclear membranes reform around the two sets.
Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm, forming two daughter cells.

written.text: Q4.2. Describe cytokinesis in animal and plant cells.
written.finalAnswer: In animal cells, a cleavage furrow forms and pinches the cytoplasm into two. In plant cells, vesicles form a cell plate between the daughter nuclei; it grows outward and develops into a new cell wall, separating the daughter cells.

rubric.why: Animal cells divide through a cleavage furrow.
rubric.how: Mention the cleavage furrow.

rubric.why: The furrow completes division by constricting the cell.
rubric.description: Explain the result in animal cells.
rubric.how: Say it pinches the cell or cytoplasm into two.

rubric.why: The cell plate is the characteristic structure in plant-cell cytokinesis.
rubric.description: State what forms in plant cells.
rubric.how: Mention cell-plate formation between daughter nuclei.

rubric.why: The plate becomes the boundary between the two daughter cells.
rubric.description: Explain how plant cells are separated.
rubric.how: State that the plate develops into a new cell wall.

modelAnswer: In an animal cell, a cleavage furrow forms in the cell membrane.
The furrow deepens and pinches the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.
In a plant cell, vesicles gather between the daughter nuclei and form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outward and develops into a new cell wall, separating the two daughter cells.

written.text: Q4.3. Describe the significance of mitosis.
written.finalAnswer: Mitosis enables growth, repair and replacement of cells, regeneration, and asexual reproduction in some organisms. It maintains the chromosome number and produces genetically identical daughter cells.

rubric.why: Mitosis increases cell number for organismal growth.
rubric.how: Mention growth.

rubric.why: Mitosis replaces damaged or worn-out cells.
rubric.how: Mention repair or cell replacement.

rubric.why: Mitosis supports regeneration and asexual reproduction in some organisms.
rubric.description: Give a further role of mitosis.
rubric.how: Mention regeneration or asexual reproduction.

rubric.why: Mitosis preserves chromosome number and genetic similarity.
rubric.description: State its outcome for daughter cells.
rubric.how: Mention identical cells or maintenance of chromosome number.

modelAnswer: Mitosis increases the number of cells and enables growth of an organism.
It replaces worn-out or damaged cells and helps in tissue repair.
It enables regeneration and serves in asexual reproduction in some organisms.
It maintains the chromosome number and produces genetically identical daughter cells.

written.text: Q4.4. Describe the events that occur during the phases of meiosis-I.
written.finalAnswer: In prophase-I homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over occurs. In metaphase-I homologous pairs line up at the equator. In anaphase-I homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles while sister chromatids remain together. In telophase-I nuclei may reform and cytokinesis produces two haploid cells, each with duplicated chromosomes.

rubric.why: Pairing and crossing over are signature events of prophase-I.
rubric.how: Mention homologous chromosome pairing and crossing over.

rubric.why: Homologous pairs align at the equator during metaphase-I.
rubric.how: State that homologous pairs line up at the equator.

rubric.why: Homologous chromosomes, rather than sister chromatids, separate in anaphase-I.
rubric.how: State that homologous chromosomes move to opposite poles.

rubric.why: The first meiotic division ends with haploid cells whose chromosomes remain duplicated.
rubric.how: Mention telophase-I or cytokinesis and the two haploid daughter cells.

modelAnswer: Prophase-I: Homologous chromosomes pair to form pairs, and crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids.
Metaphase-I: Homologous pairs line up at the equator of the cell.
Anaphase-I: Homologous chromosomes separate and move to opposite poles; sister chromatids remain attached.
Telophase-I: Nuclear membranes may reform around the chromosome sets.
Cytokinesis divides the cell, producing two haploid daughter cells with duplicated chromosomes.

written.text: Q4.5. Describe the significance of meiosis.
written.finalAnswer: Meiosis produces haploid gametes, maintains the chromosome number of a species across generations after fertilization, and creates genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment.

rubric.why: Meiosis produces haploid reproductive cells.
rubric.how: Mention haploid gametes or spores as appropriate.

rubric.why: The reduction division makes fertilization restore the diploid number.
rubric.how: State that meiosis halves the chromosome number.

rubric.why: Crossing over introduces new allele combinations.
rubric.how: Mention crossing over.

rubric.why: Meiosis creates variation within a population.
rubric.description: State the variation outcome or another mechanism.
rubric.how: Mention genetic variation or independent assortment.

modelAnswer: Meiosis produces haploid gametes with half the chromosome number of the parent cell.
After fertilization, the diploid chromosome number of the species is restored, so the chromosome number does not double in each generation.
Crossing over exchanges DNA between homologous chromosomes.
Independent assortment and crossing over produce genetic variation among offspring.

written.text: Q4.1. What role might mistakes in the cell cycle checkpoints play in the emergence of cancer?
written.finalAnswer: If checkpoints fail to stop or repair cells with damaged DNA, those cells may keep dividing. Mutations can accumulate, leading to uncontrolled cell division and cancer.

rubric.why: Checkpoint failure allows abnormal cells to pass through the cycle.
rubric.how: Explain that checkpoints fail to detect or stop damaged cells.

rubric.why: Uncontrolled division is a central feature of cancer.
rubric.description: Explain the effect on cell division.
rubric.how: State that the cells continue dividing abnormally.

rubric.why: Mutations can accumulate when damaged DNA is not repaired.
rubric.how: Mention mutations or DNA damage.

rubric.why: The question asks how checkpoint errors may lead to cancer.
rubric.how: State that uncontrolled division can result in cancer.

modelAnswer: Cell-cycle checkpoints normally detect DNA damage and can stop the cycle for repair or cause the cell to die.
If these checkpoints fail, damaged cells may continue dividing.
Mutations can then accumulate and the cells may divide uncontrollably.
This uncontrolled growth can lead to the emergence of cancer.

written.text: Q4.2. Why do skin cells divide continuously throughout an organism's existence, but nerve and muscle cells permanently exit the cell cycle?
written.finalAnswer: Skin cells are continually lost or damaged, so they divide to replace them and maintain the tissue. Mature nerve and muscle cells are highly specialized and usually remain in a non-dividing state, performing their functions rather than re-entering the cell cycle.

rubric.why: Skin cells divide to replace cells lost from the tissue.
rubric.how: Mention ongoing loss, damage or replacement.

rubric.why: Replacement maintains and repairs the skin tissue.
rubric.how: Connect cell division to tissue maintenance or repair.

rubric.why: Mature nerve and muscle cells are highly specialized.
rubric.description: Describe the cells that leave the cycle.
rubric.how: Mention their specialized mature state.

rubric.why: These mature cells usually remain outside the active cell cycle.
rubric.how: State that they usually do not re-enter the cycle.

modelAnswer: Skin cells are regularly lost or damaged, so cell division replaces them and helps maintain and repair the skin.
Mature nerve and muscle cells are highly specialized for their functions.
They usually leave the cell cycle and remain in a non-dividing state rather than producing replacement cells by division.

examTips: Short questions often ask for one phase, function or difference; use the exact stage name and a clear defining event.
Long questions commonly ask you to describe mitosis, meiosis-I, cytokinesis or the significance of a process. Organize the answer by phase or by separate points.
For mitosis, keep the order prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase. Correct stage names and events earn marks.
For a diagram question, draw clear cells and chromosomes, and label structures such as chromosomes, spindle fibres, equator, poles and nuclear membrane where relevant.
Use precise comparisons: meiosis-I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis-II separates sister chromatids. Crossing over occurs in prophase-I.

hints: Recall the phase when chromosomes are copied.
yourTurn.question: Q4.2. In which phase of cell cycle, the chromosomes duplicate?
solution: DNA replication takes place during the S phase of interphase.
Therefore, chromosomes duplicate in the S phase.

hints: Think of the mitotic stage where chromosomes move apart.
The chromatids move toward opposite poles.
yourTurn.question: Q4.3. During which phase of mitosis sister chromatids separate?
solution: Sister chromatids are pulled apart by spindle fibres.
They move towards opposite poles during anaphase.

steps.why: Prophase begins mitosis by making chromosomes visible and organizing the spindle.
steps.text: Prophase: Chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes. The spindle forms and the nuclear membrane breaks down.

steps.why: Metaphase is identified by chromosome alignment at the cell's equator.
steps.text: Metaphase: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes, which line up at the equator of the cell.

steps.why: The separation and movement of sister chromatids define anaphase.
steps.text: Anaphase: Sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.

steps.why: Telophase restores two nuclei, one around each chromosome set.
steps.text: Telophase: Chromosomes reach the poles, and nuclear membranes reform around the two sets.

steps.why: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm to complete cell division.
steps.text: Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm, forming two daughter cells.

example.question: Describe the events that occur during the phases of mitosis. Include a labelled diagram if required.
example.answer: Prophase: Chromatin condenses to form visible chromosomes. The spindle forms and the nuclear membrane breaks down. Metaphase: Spindle fibres attach to chromosomes, which line up at the equator of the cell. Anaphase: Sister chromatids separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell. Telophase: Chromosomes reach the poles, and nuclear membranes reform around the two sets. Cytokinesis then divides the cytoplasm, forming two daughter cells. Diagram description: Draw four simple cells in sequence, labelled Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase and Telophase. Show condensed chromosomes and spindle formation in prophase; chromosomes along the equator with spindle fibres in metaphase; separated chromatids moving towards opposite poles in anaphase; and two reforming nuclei in telophase. Label chromosomes, spindle fibres, equator, poles and nuclear membrane where visible.

explain.title: Interphase prepares the cell
explain.body: Interphase includes G1, S and G2. The cell grows and carries out its activities in G1, replicates DNA in S, and prepares for division in G2.

explain.title: Mitosis makes matching cells
explain.body: Mitosis is nuclear division in somatic cells. Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase lead to two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent.

explain.title: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm
explain.body: Animal cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell in two. Plant cells form a cell plate that develops into a new cell wall.

explain.title: Meiosis reduces chromosome number
explain.body: Meiosis has two divisions. Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis-I, reducing chromosome number; sister chromatids separate in meiosis-II.

explain.title: Meiosis creates variation
explain.body: Crossing over in prophase-I and independent assortment create new genetic combinations. Meiosis produces haploid cells and helps maintain a species' chromosome number after fertilization.

mistakes: Do not say DNA replication happens in mitosis; it occurs in the S phase before cell division.
Do not confuse metaphase, when chromosomes line up, with anaphase, when chromatids separate.
In meiosis-I, homologous chromosomes separate; sister chromatids remain together until meiosis-II.
Do not say mitosis halves chromosome number; it normally preserves it.
Do not describe plant cytokinesis as a cleavage furrow; plants form a cell plate.
Crossing over occurs in prophase-I of meiosis, not ordinary mitotic prophase.
